slides.label: Geometric Proof of the Metric Curvature Formula
slides.notes: Open with the chapter question: why should curvature be readable from the metric alone? The deck treats the proof as a measurement story. A tiny vector transported around a tiny loop returns rotated; the rotation is curvature times area. The metric tells us how the coordinate rulers change, and those ruler changes create exactly the circulation that the formula records.

slides.label: Metric Rulers Before Curvature
slides.notes: Before showing the curvature formula, make the metric concrete. In orthogonal coordinates, A and B are not abstract coefficients; they are the lengths of the coordinate ruler marks. The grid image asks the audience to inspect how a unit step in the map can mean different physical lengths on the surface. Curvature will come from the way these rulers vary from point to point.

slides.label: Flat Plane Zero-Curvature Dry Run
slides.notes: The flat plane is the control experiment. If the same vector is carried around a rectangle in the Euclidean plane, the edge turns cancel and the vector returns with no net rotation. This zero case matters because the curved proof will keep the same bookkeeping but replace constant rulers by changing metric rulers.

slides.label: The Connection Field Lives in the Map
slides.notes: Now introduce the connection one-form as the map-level field that tells an orthonormal frame how to rotate. In orthogonal coordinates its two coefficients are built from cross-variation of the metric scale factors: how the u-ruler changes in the v-direction and how the v-ruler changes in the u-direction. This is the first place the proof becomes metric-only.

slides.label: A Small Cell Converts Circulation to Holonomy
slides.notes: The holonomy around a small coordinate cell is the circulation of the connection around its boundary. Walking the four sides is just adding signed edge contributions. Stokes' theorem converts this boundary sum into the exterior derivative of the connection over the cell, and for a tiny cell the result is curvature times metric area.

slides.label: Let the Cell Shrink
slides.notes: The shrinking-cell picture gives the limiting logic. Large loops include accumulated variation, but as the cell collapses to a point, circulation divided by metric area settles onto the local curvature. The notebook's diagnostic curve checks the same idea numerically: limit ratios approach the invariant value near zero.

slides.label: The Metric Curvature Formula
slides.notes: Only after the circulation story is in place do we display the formula. The numerator is the divergence-like sum of two ruler-change rates, and the denominator converts coordinate area into metric area. The minus sign is an orientation convention tied to the chosen ordered frame. The important point is that no normal vector, embedding, or second fundamental form appears.

slides.label: Two Sanity Checks
slides.notes: Use two quick metrics to test the formula. Polar coordinates on the Euclidean plane have changing coordinate rulers but still zero curvature, so the formula must cancel. Latitude-longitude coordinates on the unit sphere give constant curvature one on a regular patch. These examples separate coordinate variation from genuine curvature.

slides.label: Proof Ledger and Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by turning the proof into a reusable ledger: metric scale factors define the orthonormal frame, the frame defines a connection one-form, the connection circulates around small cells, and the per-area limit is Gaussian curvature. This is the geometric content of the metric curvature formula and the local heart of Gauss's intrinsic curvature result.
